<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Brad Sherman, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Cleo Fields>: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) promotes international macroeconomic stability by providing financial assistance programs to countries in crisis, surveillance of the international economy, and technical assistance to help countries implement sound economic policies.\13\ The IMF has increased its membership from its initial 44 nations to 191 countries, although its mandate--promoting macroeconomic and financial stability--has remained unchanged since its inception. Today, the IMF focuses on three core areas: (1) emergency lending to countries in economic crisis; (2) surveillance of the global economy; and (3) technical assistance to help governments strengthen their capacity to design and implement effective financial policies.\14\
\13\IMF, About the IMF (Accessed Apr. 26, 2025).
\14\Ibid.
The IMF funds its activities primarily through ``quotas,'' which represent the monetary contribution by each country. A member country's quota generally reflects its size and position in the world economy, so larger, wealthier countries generally contribute the most and less developed countries have smaller quotas. The amount that a country contributes is also the amount that it can borrow from the IMF. Thus, the IMF likens itself to a ``credit union where members put in money to earn interest on their deposits and can also tap this pool of resources by taking out a loan.''\15\
\15\IMF, Explainer: How the IMF Finances Itself and Why it Matters for the Global Economy (Jun. 25, 2025).
A country's quota is also reflective of its vote in the IMF. Unlike other international organizations, where each country has one vote, voting power and decision-making at the IMF reflects a member country's relative economic position.\16\ The vote of each member is determined by the sum of its basic votes (which are equally distributed among all members) and quota-based votes.\17\ As the IMF increases the quotas, raising more finances for Fund activities (as has been approved on 16 occasions\18\), voting shares can (but do not always) change; in the most recent increase, for example, voting power stayed constant while the quota total increased to nearly $1 trillion, reflecting a 50% increase in what countries had previously paid in.\19\
\16\International Monetary Fund, How Does the IMF Make Decisions? (Accessed Apr. 19, 2026).
\17\Ibid.
\18\IMF, IMF Board of Governors Approves Quota Increase Under 16th General Review Quotas (Dec. 18, 2023).
\19\International Monetary Fund, IMF Executive Directors and Voting Power (Apr. 19, 2026).
This is significant in a nation's IMF engagement because major policy decisions require 85% of the total voting share. For the United States, which has the highest quota and therefore the highest voting share--16.49%, it means that the U.S. has the power to unilaterally veto all such policy decisions. Day-to-day decisions (non-policy decisions), however, at the IMF require only 50% of the voting share.\20\
\20\Rebecca Nelson, The International Monetary Fund, Congressional Research Service (Dec. 8, 2025).
Separately, the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988 requires the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury to consider whether other countries manipulate their currency ``for purposes of preventing effective balance of payments adjustments or gaining unfair competitive advantage in international trade.''\21\ In 2019, the Treasury Secretary triggered this law for the first time in over 20 years, determining that China is a currency manipulator because it allowed its currency to fall to an 11-year low.\22\ The designation, which lasted five months, was mostly symbolic, seen as a lever in a trade disagreement between the U.S. and China.\23\ Treasury is also required to report on currency manipulation every six months: In the latest report, Treasury did not designate China as a currency manipulator, although it stated that China ``stands out among major trading partners in its lack of transparency around its exchange rate policies and practices.''\24\
\21\Treasury, Treasury Designates China as a Currency Manipulator (Aug. 5, 2019).
\22\Ibid.
\23\NPR, S. Horsley, Treasury Declares China A 'Currency Manipulator,' Escalating Trade War (Aug. 5, 2019).
\24\Treasury, Treasury Releases Report on Macroeconomic and Foreign Exchange Policies of Major Trading Partners of the United States (Jan. 29, 2026).
H.R. 8290 directs Treasury to vote against IMF quota increases in the vote representation of China at the IMF, which effectively blocks all future quota increases, something Republicans on the Committee have long pursued. The bill removes the ability to negotiate future IMF quota increases, and is especially problematic in times of crisis, as happened during the COVID-19 pandemic. At that time, the IMF raised its borrowing limits and offered Rapid Credit Facility (RCF) and Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI) to help members deal with the impacts of the crisis.\25\ HFSC Democrats supported a quota increase (up to $3 trillion)\26\ as part of the ``Heroes Act''\27\ to help support the IMF's programs, and especially struggling developing countries. Unfortunately, the first Trump Administration refused to vote in support of the increase at the IMF. However, early in the Biden Administration, HFSC Democrats pressed the Treasury to vote in support of an increase, which Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen later agreed to do.\28\ The quota increase provided hundreds of millions of dollars in reserves that developing countries used to lower their borrowing costs during the crisis.\29\ Some countries went further and used their allocations to fund specific projects, like a cold storage facility for COVID vaccines in Gambia and subsidies to vulnerable households in North Macedonia.\30\
\25\IMF, Temporary Modifications To Access Limits Under The Large Natural Disaster Window Of The Rapid Credit Facility And Of The Rapid Financing Instrument (Jun. 21, 2021).
\26\116th Congress, Rep. Garcia (D-IL), H.R.6581--Robust International Response to Pandemic Act
\27\H. Rept. 116-718--REPORT ON THE ACTIVITY of the COMMITTEE ON FINANCIAL SERVICES of the UNITED STATES HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES for the ONE HUNDRED SIXTEENTH CONGRESS (Jan. 2, 2021).
\28\PBS Newshour, M. Crutsinger, IMF policy panel endorses $650 billion increase in resources (Apr. 8, 2021).
\29\IMF, Historic $650 Billion Liquidity Boost Continues to Benefit the Global Economy (Aug. 29, 2023)
\30\Ibid.
Committee Republicans, then and since, have generally rejected IMF quota increases. In the pandemic-era situation, for example, Rep. Hill labeled the push to increase IMF funding in crisis as a, ``blank check to genocidal regimes and state sponsors of terrorism.''\31\ Nothing could be further from the truth. Sanctioned countries are unable to use their reserves (e.g., Iran, which has not used any of its reserves), due, in part, to stringent U.S. and allied sanctions. China has not drawn on its reserves either and has no need to use them.\32\
\31\Rep. French Hill, Rep. Hill Introduces Bill to Stop Democrats' Blank Check to Genocidal Regimes and State Sponsors of Terrorism (Mar. 4, 2021).
\32\Center for Economic and Policy Research, Righting the Record: Claims that SDRs ``Help US Enemies'' Are Baseless--CEPR (Apr.14, 2022).
Thus, this bill works to accomplish what the majority has tried to do for years: cap the overall level of funds available for IMF activities. The bill would negatively affect the organization's ability to fulfill its mission to support economic policies that promote financial stability and monetary cooperation which are essential to increase productivity, job creation, and economic well-being.
To be clear, in the past two Congresses, Democrats and Republicans have supported efforts that target China's currency interventions: H.R. 692, the ``China Exchange Rate Transparency Act'' (Meuser), would direct the Treasury to advocate for enhanced transparency in China's exchange rate arrangements at the IMF. Additionally, that legislation called for stricter IMF oversight of China's compliance with its IMF commitments. This bill, however, would not have any effect on China, which has generally rebuffed accusations and evidence about the manipulation of its exchange rates, but instead harm the IMF itself.\33\
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 8290.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Brad Sherman,
Stephen F. Lynch,
